summary: The Meeting cost calculator works out meeting duration from the average salary, number of attendees, the time spent on setting up the meeting and the supplementary cost per meeting. It is built for a practical question that turns up in daily life. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Meeting cost calculator work?
sections.html:
The Meeting cost calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports meeting duration in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case; then you type in the average salary, number of attendees, the time spent on setting up the meeting and the supplementary cost per meeting.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Meeting cost calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Meeting duration=(-average salary × time spent on setting up the meeting + cost of meeting − supplementary cost per meeting) ÷ (average salary × number of attendees)
Frequency value=cost of meetings per year ÷ cost of meeting
Salary #2=(cost of meeting − meeting duration × salary #1 − time spent on setting up the meeting × salary #1 − supplementary cost per meeting) ÷ meeting duration
Meeting duration=(cost of meeting − time spent on setting up the meeting × salary #1 − supplementary cost per meeting) ÷ (salary #1 + salary #2 + salary #3)
Salary #2=(cost of meeting − meeting duration × (salary #1 + salary #3 + salary #4) − time spent on setting up the meeting × salary #1 − supplementary cost per meeting) ÷ meeting duration
Cost of meeting=meeting duration × salary #1 + meeting duration × salary #2 + meeting duration × salary #3 + meeting duration × salary #4 + meeting duration × salary #5 + time spent on setting up the meeting × salary #1 + supplementary cost per meeting

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Meeting cost calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the average salary, number of attendees and the time spent on setting up the meeting — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Meeting cost calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns meeting duration, derived from the average salary, number of attendees and the time spent on setting up the meeting. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Meeting cost calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the average salary, number of attendees, the time spent on setting up the meeting and the supplementary cost per meeting, which is 19 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter average salary in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Average salary opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (3 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Cost of meeting = 99000. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Meeting cost calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
